figures.caption: John Bachelder, View of Lowell, Massachusetts, 1856. Panoramic view sketched from the Tuxbury residence, Dracut Heights, across the Merrimack River, showing the brick textile mills.

books.section: Rise of Manufacturing and the Age of Jackson (1820–1845)

options.misconception: The Lowell experience shows textile manufacturing declining.
options.text: The decline of textile manufacturing in the United States

options.misconception: The Lowell experience shows enslaved labor replacing factory labor.
options.text: The replacement of factory labor by enslaved labor in the North

options.misconception: The Lowell experience shows all agricultural work ending.
options.text: The end of all agricultural work in New England
The movement of young women from farms into textile factory wage labor

rationales.A: Textile manufacturing grew; it did not decline.
rationales.B: Northern factories used wage labor, not enslaved labor.
rationales.C: Agriculture continued in New England; it did not end.
rationales.D: Lowell recruited young farm women into wage labor in textile factories, the core labor shift of the Market Revolution. That shift moved work out of the household and into the mill, where the clock set the day.
rationales.general:
1. Name who is working. Young women who left farms to tend power looms in Lowell.
2. Name the change. Farm work gave way to wage labor in textile factories.
3. Test the reversals. Manufacturing grew, Northern factories used wage labor, and farming went on.
4. Match the shift. The letter shows the Market Revolution moving labor from farms to factories.
Remember: a labor shift is named by who moves, from where, to what work.

source: original; stimulus is a paraphrase of a Lowell mill worker’s letter (early 1840s) with the Bachelder 1856 view of Lowell
stem: The experience described in the excerpt most directly reflects which of the following changes in the early nineteenth century?

stimulus.source_note: Letter attributed to a Lowell mill worker, early 1840s, paraphrased from contemporary accounts. Image: John Bachelder, View of Lowell, Massachusetts, 1856, public domain (Library of Congress, LC-DIG-pga-07376).
stimulus.text: I have worked in the Lowell mills from 5 o’clock in the morning until 7 o’clock at night. The work is hard yet many of us have improved our minds by reading and we send money home to help our families.
